doc.title: Rusty Dedrick interviewed by Monk Rowe, Ellenville, New York, June 23, 1998

title: Playing hotels in the Catskills and shrinking bands
summary: Hotel bands lost their horns; pit bands shrank similarly.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: Do you get a chance to play much these days?

No. Very, very little. I worked the hotels and this you didn’t know and now you will know, I worked here, because of a couple of reasons. A good friend of mine and a wonderful saxophone player, Milty Hisler was working here. And the band played a show, that’s all, except for a dance set at the end and maybe a couple of tunes at the end. But that was the reason I got started over here. Then one Labor Day the leader came down from Charles Slesky’s office, who owns all this stuff, and he said, “No more horns.” Well that was it. We had had three or four horns, like I don’t know if you know Roswell Rudd, you’re going to meet him later anyway. Roswell and I and the saxophone player got X’d and they have never had horns since then. What used to be a band with some horns and another band in the lounge over there, a trio, no more. It’s just now a show band itself. It’s bass, drums and piano. Now that’s pretty much a typical development up here.
It’s much like, I think for a different reason, but the pit bands that tour with musicals now have shrunk, a lot of it because of electronics.
Yeah sure. They have that in the pit and it’s replaced so many live — or at least ostensibly live — musicians.
